column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Match each term to its description.
column17: Ion :: An atom that has gained or lost electrons
column28: Protons are positive (+), neutrons have no charge (0), and electrons are negative (−). An ion is a whole atom that has gained or lost electrons, so it carries a charge.
column29: Two of these particles live in the nucleus, and one moves around it. One term is not a particle at all.

column9: Rosa draws a Bohr model of carbon. In the center she draws 6 particles marked **+** and 6 particles marked **0**. What are the particles marked **+**?
column28: The + particles in the nucleus are protons. The 0 particles are neutrons. Electrons are negative and move in shells outside the nucleus, and an ion is a whole charged atom, not a particle inside one.
column29: Which particle in the nucleus carries a positive charge?

column9: Protons and neutrons are packed together in the dense center of an atom, called the ___.
column28: The nucleus is the dense center of the atom. It holds the protons and neutrons, so almost all of the atom's mass is there. Electrons move in shells around it.
column29: It is the atom's core. The word starts with n.

column9: Electrons are the particles that atoms use to form chemical bonds.
column28: True. Bonds form when electrons are transferred from one atom to another or shared between atoms. Protons and neutrons stay in the nucleus and are not part of bonding.
column29: Which particles are on the outside of the atom, where they can meet other atoms?

column9: The six elements that make up about 99% of living things are remembered with a six-letter memory word made from their symbols. That word is ___.
column20: CHNOPS|C H N O P S|C-H-N-O-P-S|C.H.N.O.P.S.|C.H.N.O.P.S|C, H, N, O, P, S|C,H,N,O,P,S|SPONCH|CHONPS
column28: CHNOPS: carbon (C), hydrogen (H), nitrogen (N), oxygen (O), phosphorus (P), and sulfur (S). Together they make up about 99% of living things. (Some books scramble the same six letters, like SPONCH, but Mr. Erickson's word is CHNOPS.)
column29: Write the symbols of the six elements in the order Mr. Erickson lists them. The word starts with C and ends with S.

column9: Which of these elements are among the six elements that make up about 99% of living things? Select all that apply.
column28: The six main elements of life are carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulfur. Sodium (Na) and calcium (Ca) do important jobs in the body, but they are not among the six.
column29: Think of Mr. Erickson's six-letter memory word for these elements. Each letter is one element's symbol, so check each choice's symbol against it.

column9: A jeweler's ring is made of pure gold, and every atom in it is a gold atom. Which word best describes the gold?
column28: An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom. A compound needs two or more different elements bonded together, a mixture has different substances that are not bonded, and an ion is an atom that has gained or lost electrons, so it carries a charge (the gold atoms in the ring are neutral).
column29: How many kinds of atoms are in the ring?

column9: A calcium atom loses 2 electrons. Ions like this help build your bones and teeth. Which ion forms?
column28: Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the atom becomes positive. Losing 2 electrons gives a 2+ charge, written Ca²⁺. Ca²⁻ would mean gaining 2 electrons, Ca⁺ means losing only 1, and calcium-42 is an isotope (a change in neutrons), not an ion.
column29: Electrons are negative. If an atom loses negative particles, does it become more positive or more negative? How many did it lose?

column9: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
column28: True. Each proton is +1 and each electron is −1. When the numbers match, the charges cancel and the atom has no overall charge. If they don't match, the atom is an ion.
column29: What has to be true about the + and − charges for an atom to have no charge overall?

column9: In which type of bond are electrons **transferred** from one atom to another, so the two atoms end up with opposite charges that attract?
column28: In an ionic bond, one atom gives electrons to another. One becomes positive, the other negative, and the opposite charges hold them together, as in Na⁺Cl⁻ (table salt). Covalent bonds share electrons, hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between molecules, and a peptide bond is a covalent bond that links amino acids.
column29: Think about table salt: sodium hands an electron to chlorine. What is that bond called?

column9: Lactic acid, the chemical that builds up in tired muscles, has the formula C₃H₆O₃. How many **hydrogen** atoms are in one molecule of lactic acid?
column28: The subscript right after H is 6, so there are 6 hydrogen atoms (along with 3 carbon atoms and 3 oxygen atoms).
column29: Find the H in the formula and read the small number right after it.

column9: Mr. Erickson calls one element "the backbone of every macromolecule." Which element is it?
column28: Carbon forms the backbone of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen are in those molecules too, but they mostly attach to the carbon frame instead of forming it.
column29: A backbone is the long frame that the other atoms hang on. Which of these elements forms the frame of sugars, fats, proteins, and DNA?

column9: In a water molecule, the oxygen atom and each hydrogen atom **share** a pair of electrons. A bond made by sharing electrons is a ___ bond.
column28: Sharing electrons makes a covalent bond. Covalent bonds are strong and hold together every molecule in the body, like H–O–H in water. Ionic bonds transfer electrons instead of sharing them.
column29: Think of the prefix co-, as in co-workers who share a job.

column9: A molecule must contain at least two different elements.
column28: False. A molecule is two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds, and the atoms can be the same element: O₂ (oxygen gas) is a molecule made of two oxygen atoms. Needing two or more different elements is the rule for a compound, not a molecule.
column29: Does the definition of a molecule say the atoms must be different, or only that they are bonded together?

column9: Match each element symbol to its element.
column28: Na = sodium (from its Latin name, natrium), K = potassium (from kalium), P = phosphorus, S = sulfur, Ca = calcium, and Cl = chlorine. Watch out: P is phosphorus, not potassium, and S is sulfur, not sodium.
column29: Some symbols come from Latin names, so a symbol does not always start with the first letter of the element's English name.

column9: An atom has 15 protons, 16 neutrons, and 15 electrons. Atomic numbers: C = 6, H = 1, N = 7, O = 8, P = 15, S = 16. Which element is it?
column28: 15 protons = phosphorus. The atomic number is the number of protons, and it decides the element. Sulfur's atomic number (16) matches the neutron count, not the proton count. Oxygen has 8 protons and carbon has 6. The 15 electrons only tell you the atom is neutral.
column29: Only one of the three particle counts tells you which element an atom is. Which particle does the atomic number count?

column9: Carbon-14 is used to find the age of ancient bones, wood, and other once-living remains. Every carbon atom has 6 protons, and the 14 in the name is the number of protons plus neutrons. How many **neutrons** does a carbon-14 atom have?
column28: Protons + neutrons = 14, and carbon has 6 protons, so neutrons = 14 − 6 = 8. (Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons.)
column29: The 14 counts two kinds of particles. Take away the ones you already know.

column9: Oxygen-16 and oxygen-18 are two isotopes of oxygen. How are their atoms different?
column14: They have different numbers of protons
column15: They have different numbers of neutrons
column16: They have different numbers of electrons
column28: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, so they have different masses (16 vs. 18). They have the same number of protons (8), which is why both are oxygen. A change in electrons would make an ion, not an isotope.
column29: Both are still oxygen, so one particle count must stay the same. Which particle adds mass without changing the element?

column9: Which of these are **compounds**? Select all that apply.
column28: A compound has two or more different elements bonded together: water (H and O), table salt (Na and Cl), and glucose (C, H, and O). O₂ and N₂ are molecules made of only one element, so they are not compounds.
column29: Count the different element symbols in each formula. A compound needs at least two different ones.

column9: A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between a slightly positive hydrogen atom and a slightly negative ___ or nitrogen atom in a nearby molecule.
column28: Hydrogen bonds form when a slightly positive H is pulled toward a slightly negative O or N in another molecule. They are what makes water molecules stick to each other.
column29: Think of water, H₂O. Which atom in water is slightly negative?

column9: When a cell copies its DNA, the two strands must separate (unzip) while each strand stays in one piece. Which type of bond holds the two strands to each other?
column28: Hydrogen bonds hold the two DNA strands together. They are weak, so the strands can separate, while the strong covalent bonds inside each strand stay whole. Ionic bonds hold ions like Na⁺ and Cl⁻ together, and peptide bonds link amino acids in proteins.
column29: The bonds between the strands have to break easily, but the bonds inside each strand must not break. Which type of bond is easiest to break?

column9: Match each type of bond to an example.
column14: Ionic bond :: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ held together in table salt
column15: Covalent bond :: The C–C chains in sugars and fats
column16: Hydrogen bond :: One water molecule attracted to another water molecule
column28: Table salt is held together by the attraction between oppositely charged ions (ionic). Carbon atoms in sugars and fats share electrons (covalent). The weak pull between two separate water molecules is a hydrogen bond.
column29: Charged ions → think transfer. Atoms inside one molecule → think sharing. Two separate molecules → think weak attraction.

column9: Glucose, the sugar your cells burn for energy, is C₆H₁₂O₆. How many **total** atoms are in one molecule of glucose?
column29: Read the number after each element symbol, then add them together.

column9: A glass of water is made of a huge number of H₂O molecules. If you could split one water molecule apart into its atoms, what would you have?
column14: Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom
column16: A single atom of the element water
column17: One hydrogen atom and two oxygen atoms
column28: H₂O means 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom bonded together; the 2 belongs to the H, not the O. Splitting the molecule breaks those bonds and leaves the separate atoms. One water molecule is the smallest piece that is still water, so there is no smaller water molecule, and water is a compound, not an element, so there is no such thing as a water atom.
column29: The formula H₂O lists the atoms bonded together in one molecule. What is left once those bonds are broken?

column9: Sodium is a shiny metal that reacts violently with water, and chlorine is a poisonous green gas. Bonded together, they make table salt, which you sprinkle on fries. What does this show?
column14: A compound has the average properties of its elements
column15: A compound has different properties from its elements
column16: Elements lose their atoms when they form a compound
column17: A compound keeps the properties of its most reactive element
column28: Salt is safe to eat even though sodium and chlorine are both dangerous. A compound's properties are different from the elements that make it up. The atoms are still there (one sodium and one chlorine for each unit of NaCl); they are just bonded in a new way.
column29: Is table salt shiny, explosive in water, or a poisonous gas? Compare salt to each element.

column9: Match each element to one of its main jobs in living things.
column14: Nitrogen :: Found in proteins and DNA
column15: Oxygen :: Part of water and used in respiration
column16: Phosphorus :: Found in DNA, ATP, and cell membranes
column28: Nitrogen is in proteins and DNA, oxygen is in water and used in respiration, phosphorus is in DNA, ATP, and cell membranes, and sulfur is in some proteins.
column29: Start with the pair you are surest of, then match the rest by elimination. Think back to the list of the six main elements of life in the notes, where each element came with the molecules it is found in.

column9: Elements in the human body by mass: oxygen 65%, carbon 18%, hydrogen 10%, nitrogen 3%, calcium 1.5%, all others 2.5%. What **total** percent of body mass is oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen together?
column28: 65 + 18 + 10 + 3 = 96%. These four elements make up almost all of your body mass.
column29: Add only the four percents named in the question. Leave out calcium and "all others."

column9: Put these in order from **smallest** to **largest**.
column28: Proton, atom, molecule, macromolecule, cell. Protons are inside atoms. Atoms bond into molecules, small molecules link into macromolecules, and a cell is built from huge numbers of macromolecules.
column29: Each item is built from the one before it. Start with a particle found inside the atom.

column9: Glucose can be written as the chemical formula C₆H₁₂O₆ or drawn as a structural formula. What does a **structural formula** show that a chemical formula does not?
column14: Which elements are in the molecule
column15: How many atoms of each element there are
column16: Which atoms are bonded to which
column17: The total number of atoms in the molecule
column28: A structural formula is a drawing that shows which atoms are bonded to which, with a line for each bond (like H–O–H for water). The other three choices are already in the chemical formula: the symbols tell you which elements, the subscripts tell you how many atoms of each, and adding the subscripts gives the total.
column29: Think about the difference between a list of LEGO pieces and a picture of the built model.

column9: Potassium ions (K⁺) carry nerve signals. A student says K⁺ has a plus sign because the atom gained a proton. What actually happened to make K⁺?
column28: Losing one negative electron leaves one more proton than electrons, so the charge is +1. Losing two electrons would make K²⁺, a 2+ charge. Gaining an electron makes a negative ion, and neutrons have no charge, so losing one changes only the mass. The student's idea is wrong too: gaining a proton would change the element (potassium would become calcium).
column29: Changing the number of protons changes the element itself. Which particle can an atom gain or lose and still be potassium?

column9: Ammonia (NH₃) is a gas found in cleaning products. Which description is correct?
column14: A compound made of 1 nitrogen atom and 3 hydrogen atoms
column16: A compound made of 3 nitrogen atoms and 1 hydrogen atom
column17: A molecule made of only one element
column28: N has no subscript, so there is 1 nitrogen atom; H has a 3, so there are 3 hydrogen atoms. Two different elements bonded together make it a compound, not an element. The subscript belongs to the symbol right before it.
column29: A subscript counts only the symbol it follows. How many different element symbols are in NH₃?

column9: Organic compounds contain both carbon **and** hydrogen. Which of these is an organic compound?
column28: Glucose has both carbon and hydrogen, so it is organic (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids are all organic). Water has hydrogen but no carbon, carbon dioxide has carbon but no hydrogen, and table salt has neither.
column29: Check each formula for both a C and an H. Having just one of them is not enough.

column9: Marcus is drawing a Bohr model of a neutral nitrogen atom (7 protons, 7 neutrons). What belongs on the rings around the nucleus?
column14: 7 protons: 2 on the first ring and 5 on the second
column15: 7 electrons: 2 on the first ring and 5 on the second
column16: 7 electrons: 5 on the first ring and 2 on the second
column17: 7 protons: 5 on the first ring and 2 on the second
column28: The rings are electron shells (energy levels). A neutral nitrogen atom has 7 electrons to match its 7 protons. The first shell holds only 2 electrons, so the other 5 go on the second shell. Protons stay in the nucleus, and putting 5 electrons on the first ring breaks its 2-electron limit.
column29: What are the rings drawn for, the nucleus or something outside it? Then ask how many the first ring can hold.

column9: Pure silver is made only of silver atoms. If you could break a single silver atom apart, what would you get?
column28: An atom is the smallest unit that still has the element's properties. Break it apart and it is no longer silver: you get the subatomic particles, protons, neutrons, and electrons. There is no such thing as a smaller silver atom.
column29: Can you have a piece of silver smaller than the smallest piece of silver? If not, what kind of pieces must be left?

column9: Which formula shows a molecule made of exactly **three** atoms of **two** different elements?
column28: CO₂ has 1 carbon + 2 oxygen = 3 atoms of 2 different elements. O₃ has 3 atoms but only one element, NaCl has 2 atoms, and CH₄ has 5 atoms (1 C + 4 H).
column29: For each formula, count the total atoms and then count the different element symbols.

column9: Oxygen has 8 protons. Atom X has 8 protons, 10 neutrons, and 8 electrons. Atom Y has 8 protons, 8 neutrons, and 10 electrons. Which statement is correct?
column14: X is an oxygen ion, and Y is an isotope of oxygen
column15: X and Y are atoms of two different elements
column16: X and Y are both neutral oxygen atoms
column17: X is an isotope of oxygen, and Y is an oxygen ion
column28: Both have 8 protons, so both are oxygen. X has 8 electrons (neutral) but 2 extra neutrons, so it is an isotope (oxygen-18). Y has the normal 8 neutrons but 2 extra electrons, so it is an ion with a 2− charge. Changing neutrons makes an isotope; changing electrons makes an ion.
column29: Compare each atom to a normal oxygen atom (8 protons, 8 neutrons, 8 electrons). Which particle is different in X, and which is different in Y?

column9: Hydrogen's atomic number is 1, and its most common isotope is hydrogen-1. When a neutral hydrogen-1 atom loses its electron to become H⁺, what is left?
column28: Atomic number 1 means 1 proton, and a neutral atom has 1 electron to match. The 1 in hydrogen-1 counts protons + neutrons, so there are 1 − 1 = 0 neutrons. Take away the electron and all that is left is a single proton, with no neutron beside it. That is why H⁺ is often called a hydrogen ion or simply a proton. It has a +1 charge, so it is not neutral. You will see H⁺ again with acids and pH.
column29: Use the atomic number and the 1 in hydrogen-1 to find how many protons, neutrons, and electrons the atom starts with.

column9: When water boils, the molecules separate and float away as steam, but steam is still H₂O. Which bonds broke when the water boiled?
column14: The bonds between H and O inside each molecule
column15: Ionic bonds between H⁺ and O²⁻ ions
column16: The hydrogen bonds between water molecules
column17: The bonds that hold protons in each nucleus
column28: Steam is still H₂O, so the strong covalent bonds inside each molecule did not break. Boiling only pulled the molecules away from each other by breaking the weak hydrogen bonds between them. Water is not made of ions, and boiling never touches the nucleus.
column29: If the bonds inside each molecule broke, would it still be H₂O?

column9: Chlorine's atomic number is 17. In table salt, a chlorine-37 atom gains 1 electron to become Cl⁻. How many **electrons** does this Cl⁻ ion have?
column28: The atomic number, 17, is the number of protons, and a neutral atom has the same number of electrons: 17. Cl⁻ gained 1 electron, so it has 17 + 1 = 18. The 37 is protons + neutrons (17 + 20), and neutrons do not change the electron count. With 17 protons (+) and 18 electrons (−), the charge is 1−.
column29: Which number tells you the protons, the 17 or the 37? How many electrons does a neutral chlorine atom have, and did Cl⁻ end up with more or fewer?

column9: Magnesium ions (Mg²⁺) help many of your enzymes work. A Mg²⁺ ion has 10 electrons. How many **protons** does it have?
column28: A 2+ charge means the ion has 2 more protons (+) than electrons (−), because the atom lost 2 electrons when it became an ion. 10 + 2 = 12 protons, which is magnesium's atomic number. Subtracting to get 8 would mean 8 protons and 10 electrons, a 2− charge (and 8 protons is oxygen, not magnesium).
column29: Does the 2+ mean the ion has more protons or more electrons? By how many?

column9: Jordan says hydrogen bonds are so weak that they don't matter to living things. Which evidence best argues against him?
column14: Many hydrogen bonds make water stick to itself and hold proteins in shape
column15: Hydrogen bonds hold the H and O atoms together inside each water molecule
column16: Hydrogen bonds hold Na⁺ and Cl⁻ together in a crystal of table salt
column17: Hydrogen bonds link the carbon atoms in the chains of sugars and fats
column28: Only a is true. One hydrogen bond is weak, but billions of them together are powerful: they make water stick to water and help hold proteins (and DNA) in shape. The other choices name bonds that really matter to life, but they are the wrong type: the bonds inside a water molecule and the C–C bonds in sugars and fats are covalent, and Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in salt are held by ionic bonds.
column29: Which choice describes something a hydrogen bond really does, and why that matters for life?

column9: Glycerol, part of a fat molecule, has the formula C₃H₈O₃. Which statement is true?
column14: It is a compound with 3 elements and 3 atoms
column15: It is a compound with 3 elements and 14 atoms
column16: It is an element because it is a single molecule
column17: It is a compound with 14 different elements
column28: There are 3 different symbols (C, H, O), so 3 elements, which makes it a compound. Atoms: 3 + 8 + 3 = 14. Getting 3 atoms comes from counting each symbol once and ignoring the subscripts. A single molecule can still be a compound, and 14 is the number of atoms, not elements.
column29: Count the different symbols for the number of elements. Then add every subscript for the number of atoms.

column9: Put these steps in order to describe how table salt (NaCl) forms.
column14: The opposite charges attract each other
column15: Sodium transfers one electron to chlorine
column16: Many Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions pack into a salt crystal
column17: Sodium becomes Na⁺ and chlorine becomes Cl⁻
column28: First the electron moves from sodium to chlorine. That makes sodium positive (Na⁺) and chlorine negative (Cl⁻). Opposite charges attract, and that attraction is the ionic bond. Huge numbers of ions held together this way pack into a salt crystal.
column29: Ask what must exist before anything can attract, and what must happen before sodium or chlorine can have a charge.

column9: Which row correctly gives one example of each, in this order: an element, a molecule that is **not** a compound, and a compound?
column28: Row c works: iron is one kind of atom (an element), chlorine gas is two bonded chlorine atoms (a molecule of one element, so not a compound), and methane has two different elements, C and H, bonded together (a compound). Row a starts with carbon dioxide, which has two elements, so it is a compound, not an element. Row b puts hydrogen peroxide in the middle, but H₂O₂ has two different elements, so it is a compound. Row d ends with hydrogen gas, which has only one element, so it is not a compound.
column29: Check each spot one at a time. A compound needs two or more different element symbols.

column9: Carbon-14 forms different kinds of bonds than carbon-12 because it has two extra neutrons.
column28: False. Bonding depends on electrons, and both isotopes have 6 protons and 6 electrons. The two extra neutrons in carbon-14 (8 vs. 6) change its mass, not how it bonds. Carbon-14 is radioactive, which is why it can date ancient remains up to about 50,000 years old, but it bonds just like carbon-12.
column29: Which particles take part in bonding? Are those different between the two isotopes?

column9: High in the atmosphere, a neutron slams into the nucleus of a nitrogen-14 atom (7 protons, 7 neutrons). The nucleus absorbs the neutron and then gives off one proton. Atomic numbers: C = 6, N = 7, O = 8. What kind of atom does the nucleus belong to now?
column28: Start: 7 protons, 7 neutrons. Absorbing a neutron gives 7 protons and 8 neutrons. Giving off a proton leaves 6 protons and 8 neutrons. 6 protons means carbon, and 6 + 8 = 14, so it is carbon-14 (this is how the carbon-14 used to date ancient remains forms). Nitrogen-15 counts the neutron that was added but forgets the proton that was given off (7 + 8 = 15), carbon-13 forgets the neutron that was added, and oxygen-16 adds a proton instead of taking one away.
column29: Track the protons and the neutrons one step at a time. Which count decides the element, and which two counts add up to the number in the name?

column9: A carbon atom has 4 electrons in its outer shell, with room for 4 more, so each carbon atom can form 4 covalent bonds. Why is that so important for living things?
column14: It can bond to many atoms at once, building long chains and rings
column15: Its four bonds are weak, so its molecules break apart easily for energy
column16: It can bond only to other carbon atoms, so it builds pure carbon chains
column17: Carbon atoms are so light that the molecules they build stay small
column28: Four bonds let each carbon connect to other carbons and to H, O, N, and more in several directions, building the long chains and rings of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Covalent bonds are strong, not weak; carbon bonds to many elements, not only to itself; and carbon molecules can be huge.
column29: Picture a LEGO brick with 4 connection points versus one with only 1. Which can build bigger structures?

column9: Mia's lunch has potato chips sprinkled with salt crystals (NaCl), nitrogen gas (N₂) that fills the chip bag to keep the chips fresh, a bottle of water (H₂O), and a cookie made with table sugar (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁). Which of these substances are **compounds** held together by **covalent** bonds? Select all that apply.
column28: Water (H and O) and table sugar (C, H, and O) pass both tests: each has two or more different elements, and their atoms share electrons. Salt is a compound, but sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, so its bond is ionic, not covalent. Nitrogen gas is held together by a covalent bond, but both atoms are nitrogen, so it is a molecule, not a compound.
column29: Each substance has to pass two tests. Does it have two or more different elements? Are its electrons shared between atoms, or handed from one atom to another?

column9: Elements in the human body by mass: oxygen 65%, carbon 18%, hydrogen 10%, nitrogen 3%, calcium 1.5%, all others 2.5%. Devin says this list proves there are more oxygen atoms in your body than any other kind of atom. What is wrong with his reasoning?
column14: Carbon atoms are the most numerous, because carbon is in every organic molecule
column15: An element hidden in the 2.5% of other elements could have the most atoms
column16: The list shows mass, and hydrogen atoms are so light that they are the most numerous
column17: Oxygen atoms are locked inside water molecules, so they can't be counted as atoms
column28: The list compares mass, not number of atoms. A hydrogen atom is the lightest atom (about 1/16 the mass of an oxygen atom), so even though hydrogen is only 10% of the mass, hydrogen atoms are the most common atoms in the body. Carbon is in every organic molecule, but a carbon atom is about 12 times heavier than a hydrogen atom, so there are fewer of them. The other elements are only 2.5% of the mass and are heavier atoms, so none of them can have the most atoms. Atoms bonded inside water molecules still count as atoms.
column29: A pound of feathers and a pound of bricks have the same mass. Do they have the same number of pieces? Apply that idea to atoms.

column9: A normal nitrogen atom has 7 protons, 7 neutrons, and 7 electrons. Which of these atoms or ions would **still be nitrogen**? Select all that apply.
column28: Anything with 7 protons is nitrogen. 7p/8n/7e and 7p/6n/7e are isotopes of nitrogen, and 7p/7n/10e is a nitrogen ion (3−). 8 protons is oxygen and 6 protons is carbon, no matter what the neutrons and electrons are.
column29: Which particle count is the atomic number? What do changes in the other two counts make: a new element, or something else?
